items.text: Masking isn't a single act. It's cumulative debt. The collapse doesn't mean you're weak — it means the account finally hit zero.
items.rationale: Sharp, quotable frame that replaces shame with a structural explanation. The energy-account metaphor is immediately legible with zero clinical framing required.

items.text: It's not that you can't cope. It's that no one told you the account was empty — or that you'd been borrowing from it since childhood.
items.rationale: Second variation on the masking-debt angle; opens with the internal narrative autistic adults carry ('can't cope') and redirects immediately to structural cause. Evergreen, no stat needed.

items.text: Rest doesn't end autistic burnout if nothing that caused it changes. Rest is a pause between cycles. Structural change is the exit.
items.rationale: Directly challenges 'have you tried resting?' without dismissing rest itself; gives people a frame to bring to therapists, partners, or employers. Grounded in 2026 active discourse.

items.text: 'Listen to your body' is genuinely, neurologically hard for some autistic people. The signals don't arrive on time — or at all. That's not self-neglect. That's interoception.
items.rationale: Names something the community experiences intensely but rarely sees articulated outside clinical settings. 'Some autistic people' keeps it properly scoped rather than universalising.
items.sensitivity_flag: 'Neurologically hard' reads slightly clinical; it's accurate and defensible but worth checking it doesn't land as a diagnostic claim in isolation.

items.text: If you can't reliably read your own hunger, fatigue, or overwhelm — external cues aren't a crutch. Alarms, check-ins, prompts: they're scaffolding for what your nervous system doesn't send automatically.
items.rationale: Translates the interoception insight into immediate, usable guidance. 'Scaffolding' reframes accommodation as architecture rather than weakness.

items.text: 'Pathological Demand Avoidance' vs. 'Persistent Drive for Autonomy' — same child, different lens. Does the name you use change how you show up?
items.rationale: Presents both terms neutrally and asks a practical question that invites reflection without dunking on either camp. Self-contained and opens genuine conversation.

items.text: One name frames the child as the problem. The other frames an unmet need. That distinction isn't just semantics — it changes what you're actually trying to solve.
items.rationale: Makes the stakes of the naming debate concrete and actionable for parents and educators without prescribing which term to adopt.

items.text: Have you ever not asked for an accommodation because of what it might cost you? You're not alone — 70% of neurodivergent employees fear workplace disclosure despite legal protections.
items.rationale: Uses the freshest data point in the briefing (Forbes, June 24 2026) to invite low-risk disclosure in replies. Question form lowers the engagement barrier.
items.sensitivity_flag: The 70% figure comes from a Forbes-cited survey; verify exact methodology and sample size before posting — the stat is defensible from the briefing but confirm it isn't rounded or recontextualised.

items.text: Knowing your rights and feeling safe to use them aren't the same thing. For a lot of neurodivergent people at work, that gap is the whole problem.
items.rationale: Evergreen reframe of the disclosure-safety gap — high recognition, no stat required. Pairs naturally with the question post if scheduling both from this angle.

items.text: You had a genuinely good time. And you're wrecked for days afterward. That's not a failure to recover — that's the cost of real-time decoding, masking, and sensory management for hours.
items.rationale: Opens with the paradox the community lives and names the mechanism precisely, giving people language to explain it to others without moralising about recovery speed.

items.text: AuDHD burnout isn't double the burnout. It's two systems in direct conflict — one revving, one shutting down, at the same time.
items.rationale: Short, quotable, extremely high recognition for the AuDHD audience. Describes an under-named experience that neither ADHD nor autism content alone captures.

items.text: Low-demand parenting works. A 2026 study found parental stress stays dangerously high even when it does. You're doing the right thing. What helps you regulate while you do that for someone else?
items.rationale: Validates PDA parents with published research, then opens a practical conversation — fills a real gap where community advice rarely acknowledges the personal cost of the approach.
items.sensitivity_flag: 'Dangerously high' is the briefing's characterisation of the PMC study's language; verify the paper's exact wording before posting to confirm the claim isn't inadvertently exaggerated.
